name: Microsoft 365 and Google Docs Basics
objectives: Using Google Docs or Word on the web, open a new blank document, give it a clear name and say where it is saved, with a name that says what the file is and the right online storage named (Google Drive or OneDrive)

chapters.name: Chapter 1: Writing and sharing a document

lessons.title: Lesson 1: Opening Google Docs or Word on the web
lessons.text:
Lesson 1 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Open a new blank document, give it a name and know where it is saved.
This lesson builds toward: Using Google Docs or Word on the web, you will open a new blank document, give it a clear name and say where it is saved, with a name that says what the file is and the right online storage named (Google Drive or OneDrive).
Google Docs is free with a Google account (the same account as Gmail). Go to docs.google.com and choose Blank document. Microsoft Word on the web is free with a Microsoft account (the same account as Outlook.com). Go to microsoft365.com, choose Word, then Blank document.
Both save your work by themselves as you type. Google keeps it in Google Drive; Microsoft keeps it in OneDrive. Both are online storage, also called the cloud, so you can open the file again from any computer or phone after you sign in.
Give every file a clear name at the top left, such as "Volunteer Day Flyer - May". Clear names make files easy to find later.
Step by step:
- Go to docs.google.com (Google) or microsoft365.com (Microsoft) and sign in.
- Choose a blank document.
- Click the name at the top left and type a clear file name.
- Type a sentence and watch for the saved message near the top.
Words to know:
- Cloud: storage on the internet, so you can reach your files from any device after you sign in.
- Google Drive / OneDrive: Google's and Microsoft's online storage, where your files are kept.
- Account: your sign-in name and password for a service.
Official sources:
- Microsoft: free Word, Excel and PowerPoint for the web
- Google Docs
Try it now: Open a blank document in Google Docs or Word on the web. Name it "My Practice Document" and type one sentence about your week.
You can now open a new document, name it and know it saves to the cloud by itself.

options: Online storage you can reach from any device after you sign in
A folder that only exists on one computer
A paid app you must buy
check.why: Google Drive and OneDrive are online storage, also called the cloud.

check.q: You typed a letter in Google Docs and want to find it again next week. What would you do now?
options: Print it so you do not lose it
Click the name at the top left and type a clear name such as "Letter to Landlord - June"
Copy it into an email to yourself
check.why: A clear file name makes the document easy to find later.

lessons.title: Lesson 2: Making a document look neat
lessons.text:
Lesson 2 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Format a title, a list and body text so a page is easy to read.
This lesson builds toward: Given a page of plain text, you will format a title, a bulleted list and body text so the page is easy to read, with the title in Heading 1, a bulleted list and one bold word.
Formatting means changing how text looks. First select the text: hold the mouse button down and drag across it, or double-click a word. Then use the toolbar at the top: B for bold, I for italic, the size box to make text bigger, and the list buttons for bullets or numbers.
Use a Heading style for titles. In the toolbar find the box that says "Normal text" (Google) or "Normal" (Word) and choose Heading 1. Headings look neat and help screen readers.
Keep it simple: one easy-to-read font, size 11 to 14 for body text, a bold title, short paragraphs and bulleted lists. If you make a mistake, press Ctrl+Z (Command+Z on a Mac) to undo.
Step by step:
- Select the text you want to change.
- Choose Heading 1 for the title.
- Select a few lines and click the bulleted list button.
- Use B to make a key word bold.
- Press Ctrl+Z (Command+Z on Mac) to undo a mistake.
Words to know:
- Formatting: changing how text looks: size, bold, lists, headings.
- Select: mark text by dragging across it so you can change it.
- Toolbar: the row of buttons at the top of the app.
Try it now: In your practice document, type a title and three items, such as three things to bring to a family picnic. Make the title Heading 1, make the items a bulleted list, and make one word bold.
You can now format a page with a heading, a bulleted list and bold text.

check.q: Which text size does the lesson suggest for body text?
check.why: Size 11 to 14 is easy to read for body text.

check.q: You want three lines to become a bulleted list. What would you do first?
options: Change the font for the whole page
check.why: You select text first, then choose the bulleted list button.

lessons.title: Lesson 3: Sharing safely and using comments
lessons.text:
Lesson 3 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Share a document with one person at the right access level and leave a comment.
This lesson builds toward: Given a document and a person who needs to see it, you will share the document at the lowest access level the person needs and leave a comment, choosing the right level every time and never using "Anyone with the link" for private details.
Both apps have a Share button at the top right. Type the person's email address and choose what they can do: view only (read), comment (suggest), or edit (change the file). Give the lowest level the person needs.
Be careful with "Anyone with the link". Anyone who gets the link, even by forwarding, can open the file. Do not use it for files with private details such as addresses, ID numbers or health information.
Comments let people give feedback without changing your words. Select some text, then choose the comment button (a speech bubble) or right-click and choose Comment. When the issue is fixed, choose Resolve.
Step by step:
- Click Share at the top right.
- Type the person's email address.
- Choose View, Comment or Edit; pick the lowest level they need.
- Send.
- To comment: select text, choose Comment, type, then post it.
Words to know:
- Share: let another person open your file.
- Access level: what a person can do with your file: view, comment or edit.
- Comment: a note on the side of the file that does not change the text.
Try it now: Share your practice document with a friend or family member as view only. Then add a comment to your title that says "Is this title clear?"
You can now share a document at the right access level and use comments for feedback.

check.q: Which access level lets someone change the words in your file?
check.why: Edit lets the person change the file; view and comment do not.

check.q: A friend fixed the problem you raised in a comment. What would you do with the comment?
options: Share the file with Anyone with the link
Leave a new comment on every line
check.why: Resolve closes a comment once the issue is fixed.

lessons.title: Lesson 4: Your first spreadsheet
lessons.text:
Lesson 4 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Make a spreadsheet with headings and five rows of data.
This lesson builds toward: Using Google Sheets or Excel on the web, you will create a spreadsheet with headings in row 1 and five rows of data, with one item per row and numbers typed without words.
A spreadsheet is a grid of boxes for lists and numbers. Google's is Sheets (sheets.google.com); Microsoft's is Excel (choose Excel at microsoft365.com). It is great for budgets, sign-up lists, schedules and inventories.
Columns go up and down and have letters (A, B, C). Rows go across and have numbers (1, 2, 3). Each box is a cell, named by its column and row, so B2 is column B, row 2.
Put headings in row 1, like "Item" in A1 and "Cost" in B1. Then type one thing per row underneath. Type numbers without words (12.50, not "12.50 dollars") so the spreadsheet can do math with them.
Step by step:
- Open Google Sheets or Excel on the web and choose a blank spreadsheet.
- Name the file.
- Type headings in row 1 (A1: Item, B1: Cost).
- Type five items in column A and their costs in column B.
- Make row 1 bold.
Words to know:
- Spreadsheet: a grid of cells for lists and numbers, like Google Sheets or Excel.
- Cell: one box in a spreadsheet, named by column letter and row number, like B2.
- Column / row: columns go up and down (letters); rows go across (numbers).
Try it now: Make a spreadsheet called "Practice Budget". Put Item and Cost in row 1, then five real costs for a week or an event, such as groceries, bus fare or decorations.
You can now set up a spreadsheet with headings and rows of data.

check.q: In a spreadsheet, what is a cell?
options: One box, named by its column and row
The file name at the top
check.why: Each box is a cell, such as B2 for column B, row 2.

check.q: You are making a sign-up list. Where would you type the headings "Name" and "Phone"?
options: At the bottom of the sheet
In row 1, one heading per column
check.why: Headings go in row 1, with one thing per row underneath.

lessons.title: Lesson 5: Adding it up with a formula
lessons.text:
Lesson 5 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Use SUM to total a column so it updates by itself.
This lesson builds toward: Given a column of numbers in a spreadsheet, you will write a SUM formula that totals the column and updates by itself, with a correct total that changes when a number is changed.
A formula tells the spreadsheet to do math. Every formula starts with an equals sign (=). To add cells B2 through B6, click an empty cell under them and type =SUM(B2:B6), then press Enter.
The colon means "through", so B2:B6 is B2, B3, B4, B5 and B6. If you change a number, the total changes by itself. That is the big advantage over a calculator.
Other simple formulas: =AVERAGE(B2:B6) gives the average, and =B2*2 doubles one cell. If you see an error like #NAME?, check the spelling and the equals sign.
Step by step:
- Click the empty cell under your numbers.
- Type =SUM(B2:B6) using your own cell range.
- Press Enter.
- Change one number and watch the total update.
- Type the word Total in the cell to its left.
Words to know:
- Formula: an instruction that starts with = and tells the spreadsheet to calculate.
- SUM: a formula that adds up a group of cells.
- Range: a group of cells, written like B2:B6 (B2 through B6).
Try it now: In your Practice Budget, type Total in A7 and =SUM(B2:B6) in B7. Then change one cost and check that the total changes.
You can now total a column with SUM and know the total updates when numbers change.

check.q: What is the big advantage of a SUM formula over adding on a calculator?
options: The total updates by itself when a number changes
It turns the sheet into a PDF
It shares the file with others
check.why: A formula recalculates whenever a number in its range changes.

check.q: Your costs are in B2 to B8. What would you type in B9 to total them?
check.why: =SUM(B2:B8) adds B2 through B8; =B2+B8 adds only two cells.

lessons.title: Lesson 6: Saving as PDF and printing
lessons.text:
Lesson 6 of 6 · about 4 minutes
Goal: Download a document or spreadsheet as a PDF and print it.
This lesson builds toward: Given a finished document or spreadsheet, you will download it as a PDF and print it after checking the preview, with the PDF found in the Downloads folder and nothing cut off in the preview.
A PDF is a file that looks the same on every phone and computer, and people cannot easily change it. Many job applications, offices and schools ask for PDFs.
In Google Docs or Sheets: open the File menu, choose Download, then PDF. In Word or Excel on the web: open the File menu and look for Save as or Download, then choose PDF. The file goes to your Downloads folder.
To print, open the File menu and choose Print, or press Ctrl+P (Command+P on a Mac). Check the preview first so nothing is cut off. At a library, ask staff how printing is paid for.
Step by step:
- Open the File menu.
- Choose Download (Google) or Save as / Download (Microsoft).
- Choose PDF.
- Find the file in your Downloads folder.
- To print: Ctrl+P (Command+P on Mac), check the preview, then print.
Words to know:
- PDF: a file type that looks the same everywhere and is hard to change.
- Downloads folder: the place on a computer where downloaded files go.
Try it now: Final task: make a one-page flyer or letter with a heading, a bulleted list and a contact line, plus a five-cost spreadsheet with a SUM total. Share the document as view only, then download both as PDFs.
You can now finish a document and a spreadsheet, share them safely and save them as PDFs.
How your final task is checked:
What we look at Not yet Meets Exceeds Neat one-page document The title, the bulleted list or the contact line is missing. A bold Heading 1 title, a bulleted list and a contact line, all on one page. Also uses one easy font, short paragraphs and a clear file name. Safe sharing The document is not shared, or it is shared with edit access or "Anyone with the link". Shared with one person as view only. Also leaves a comment asking for feedback and resolves it after a reply. Spreadsheet Headings are missing or fewer than five costs are listed. Item and Cost headings in row 1 and at least five costs, one per row, typed as numbers. Row 1 is bold and the file has a clear name. SUM total The total is typed by hand or the formula gives an error. A SUM formula gives the right total and updates when a cost changes. Also labels the total and adds an AVERAGE formula. PDFs One or both files are not saved as PDFs. Both the document and the spreadsheet are downloaded as PDFs and can be found in Downloads. Also checks the print preview so nothing is cut off. To pass: Meets or Exceeds on every row. If a row is Not yet, fix that part and try again.

check.q: Where does a downloaded PDF usually go?
check.why: Downloaded files go to the Downloads folder on your device.

check.q: You are about to print a flyer at the library. What would you do first?
options: Check the print preview so nothing is cut off
Change the file to a spreadsheet
check.why: The preview shows whether anything is cut off before you pay to print.
